The Children's Flight

By: Ben Dwork | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Volunteer pilots prepare for hundreds of children from all over Johannesburg -- to take to the sky for the first time and inspire a generation of children with the gift of flight.

Unique Selling Point:
Working closely with the co-founders of the Children’s Flight, we’ll get access to various flights throughout the event, as well as coordinate having camera crew accompanying our young case studies as they take to the skies for the very first time.

Summary:
Many people don’t think anything of hopping on a flight to Cape Town or Durban for the weekend. But for underprivileged children around Johannesburg, just getting to set foot on an airfield can be an awe-striking experience and a dream come true. The organizers behind The Children’s Flight aim to do just that with their annual event. Children from all parts of Johannesburg, all backgrounds, and all abilities are invited to the airport to experience their first flight. Felix Gosher and Michael Ferguson, the co-founders of the event, say it’s nearly tripled in size since last year (from 126 kids to nearly 400), and the response from the community has been truly remarkable.

In this segment, we’ll spend a day in the life with two young people living in difficult circumstances -- 16 year old Doris in the mining township of Durban deep, whose mother has polio, and her family unable to pay her school fees; and 8 year old Chimdiebere, deaf since birth and living in Tembisa with a large family that often overlooks him, leaving him with rarely enough on the table to keep him from being hungry. Overcoming very difficult odds, they both excel in their studies, have dreams for professional careers (Doris as an astronaut and Chimdiebere as a policeman) and will be taking part in the Children’s Flight on 1 September. We’ll be with them the first time they set foot on an airplane and have an up close and personal look at how this experience inspires them in their personal lives to keep reaching for their dreams.

Further information:
On the outskirts of Johannesburg in the township of Durban Deep lives sixteen year old Doris. Living in a garage by a row of old mining houses, Doris and her family do not have electricity or water. Her mother has polio, and recently, Doris was thrown out of school after her family was unable to pay the fees. However, after her story spread around the community, a good Samaritan stepped up to pay the fees and get Doris back in school. The local newspaper, the Roodeport Record, picked up on the story, and another school actually offered to sponsor Doris’s fees, uniform, and transport. Against many odds, Doris still attends school regularly and has dreams of becoming an astronaut. On Friday, 1 September, Doris will take one step closer to realizing her dream when she and hundreds of other children from in and around Johannesburg descend on Grand Central Airport in Midrand for the Children’s Flight.

Organized by career pilot Felix Gosher and his close friend, musician Michael Ferguson, the Children’s Flight is a Mandela Day initiative to “Fly, Feed, Love, Inspire” underprivileged children from various backgrounds and let them experience aviation up close, as well as see the world from a different perspective. Michael and Felix each credit each other with the origin of the event, but the story goes that Michael was inspired to write a song, “Paper Planes,” after hearing about Felix’s travels across Africa. The song is the story of a child with a dream to fly. Felix says he would land his airplane in various remote parts of the continent and would always be struck by how children would run up to it, amazed by the fact that it seemed to defy gravity and take him off to exotic places. According to Michael, “We didn’t plan on writing that song… he told me his story about becoming a pilot, and after that, we just sort of wrote [it].” Both Felix and Michael were satisfied with the final product, but initially, nothing more came of it. It was only on a work trip flying through central Africa that Felix realized, what good is inspiration if you don’t share it with others? From there, he and Michael decided that the thing they could give others was the gift of flight, and thus the Children’s Flight was born.

Now in its second year, the event has nearly tripled in size (400 kids will attend in 2017), and the energy amongst the youngsters is palpable. They come from all parts of the city. Chimdiebere is 8 years old, and this will be his first time flying. His favorite subject in school is math, and he wants to be a policeman when he grows up. He lives with his large family in Tembisa, up to eight members sharing the same small house, and makes the long commute in to school every day in Illovo. However, Chimdiebere’s experience will be different than most other kids, because he’s deaf. Though he has 2 cochlear implants, he can only hear very loud noises (dogs barking, doors slamming, and airplanes). At St Vincent’s School for the Deaf, where he attends, the teachers have to make sure he’s eaten and can function properly for the day, because food is scarce at home. Often, the only meals he will get for the day will be at the school. His family doesn’t use sign language, so when he goes home, there’s no one to talk to, and he typically only plays with his baby brother. In spite of all this, he’s doing very well in school and is quite popular.

An event like Children’s Flight brings together kids like Doris and Chimdiebere, and the pilots and other volunteers who give their time hope that it will inspire them to dream and understand that dreams can be within striking distance if you work at it. Pilots like Werner Nel demonstrate that. He began training to become a pilot in 2007. His career began as a private pilot with the ultimate goal of becoming a commercial pilot. However, in October 2009, he was involved in a motorcycle accident that nearly took his life. Though he survived, doctors had to amputate his right leg. He was devastated at the prospect that his flying career may be over. But he didn’t let that stop him. After three years of physical therapy and numerous operations, he gained his commercial pilot’s license in 2012 and secured a job as a pilot instructor. He is still able to fly and now also works as an aerobatic pilot. His advice to anyone who asks about his experience -- and especially the kids who will be at Children’s Flight -- is: “Never give up and always remember, if you give your 100%, you will have endless possibilities.”

Press Release:


For many of us taking a flight has become quite routine and we even complain about all the travel. But for many of the country’s children, watching the planes flying overhead is as close to taking to the skies as they will get. But a pilot and a musician decided to change that and provide a beacon of hope. Claire Mawisa has the story.

Script:


00:00 - 00:21 - MUSIC CUE: FLYING KITES
VO: On the outskirts of Johannesburg near an old mining settlement near Roodeport lives 18 year old Doris Gondwe. Doris and her family’s home does not have water or electricity, but despite her circumstances, Doris has grand aspirations.
DORIS GONDWE (DG): I would like to be an astronaut one day.
CLAIRE MAWISA (CM): Why do you want to be an astronaut? That’s fantastic.
DG: I think it is because of curiosity, ambition, and the adventure spirit that I have.
CM: Tell me about school. Do you enjoy school? What are you favorite subjects?
DG: My favorite subjects are physical sciences, English, and life sciences.
VO: It’s that spirit that has helped Doris climb to the top of her class.
Sound up footage - Taren Welthagen and Doris. Taren: See I told you the thing with history is all you need to do is learn, Doris.
VO: Taren Welthagen runs CLAW, an animal welfare program headquartered near Doris’s home. Taren and her family also help look out for local families and their kids.
TAREN WELTHAGEN (TW): Doris is one of the families we’ve been looking after for quite a few years. We always believe that with one you can’t have the other. So with a dog, you’ve got the person behind the dog. We still check in on the family, and we provide food parcels when we can. She’s incredibly humble, um, always thinking about others before she thinks about herself. I went to go fetch her from school, and I had bought a sandwich for her. And I noticed she had sort of nibbled on half the sandwich. She had kept the other half for her mom when she got home, so to think about your mom and everyone before yourself, I think it’s something incredibly special.
VO: Soon, through The Children’s Flight, a special initiative to bring air travel to underprivileged kids, Doris will have the opportunity to fly for the first time.
CM: What did they tell you when they told you about The Children’s Flight?
DG: I couldn’t believe it at first. I actually asked her like five times, “Really, am I going to be flying?” “Yes.” And I was like, “No.” I was overwhelmed. I was excited. I just couldn’t contain myself. Because, like, I never thought that I would really, like, fly at this age and, yeah. I thought maybe I would fly when I’m working and older.
VO: Meanwhile, on the other side of Johannesburg, we met 8 year old Chimdiebere, a learner at St Vincent School for the Deaf, who will also be taking part in The Children’s Flight.
CM: Does anyone at home know how to sign?
CHIMDIEBERE (CH) (Voice through interpreter): They sign a little bit but not much. Well, my family they all talking, and I’m asking them, what’s happening? Why are you all talking? That’s not how I talk.
CM: What is going to happen tomorrow?
CH: Tomorrow, tomorrow… where are we going? We’re flying tomorrow.
VO: Veronica Tesner is one of Chimdiebere’s teachers at St Vincent.
CM: How long have you been working with Chimdiebere?
VERONICA TESNER (VT): Well, he started school in 2015, and when he came to school, he was frustrated. He was a difficult child then, I think, because of no language. But since he’s been here, things has been so much easier. Easier to communicate with him. It’s easier to interact with him, because he’s got the ability to understand sign language.
VO: Communication is just one of the challenges Chimdiebere’s family has faced. His grandmother explains.
COSHNAH MTSHAGI (CO) (Translated from Xhosa): It’s hard, we are poor. Chimde wanted to go to school but his mother is unemployed. His mother chose to leave him with me. As his grandmother, I do everything his mother did. Getting food was not easy until we came to the school. They provided us with food parcels on Fridays.
CM: How do you feel about him having this great opportunity to fly for the first time?
CO: Mama, in my family, Chimde is a blessing. I never fly, even though I want to fly. I need money in an airplane. I never enter an airplane. It is a blessing from God. I am very happy.
04:05 - 04:17 - MUSIC CUE: HERDING CLOUDS
VO: Felix Gosher is a contract pilot for the United Nations. He helps deliver food and medicine to the rural areas of Central Africa.
CM: How is your reception with regard to the kids when they see you flying an aircraft?
FELIX GOSHER (FG): When those Central African kids, and the South Sudanese kids that we’ve also done contract in, when they see the airplane, they’re completely inspired. They look at us in wonder. They approach the aircraft, because they’re fascinated by the big metal bird, and they want to be part of the experience. And that’s very much the founding area of this initiative.
CM LINK: Organized by Felix Gosher and his friend musician Michael Ferguson, The Children’s Flight is an initiative to “Fly, Feed, Love, Inspire.” For many children, this is their first time ever on an airplane.
VO: Michael Ferguson, co-founder of The Children’s Flight, explains further.
CM: Why children and airplanes?
MICHAEL FERGUSON (MF): Aviation is such a beacon of hope. Last year, we had some younger children. And some people say, “Man, these kids probably don’t get what’s happening. And they won’t remember the experience.” But I don’t believe that’s true. I think subconsciously, you take away something much bigger. I think it’s got such a lifelong impact on the children.
VO: On 1 September, at Grand Central Airport in Midrand, Felix and Michael’s initiative took to the skies.
CM LINK: Children come from all parts of Johannesburg to attend The Children’s Flight, representing different schools, organizations, and centers. Since the inaugural event last year, the event has almost tripled in size.
05:25 - 06:50 - MUSIC CUE: FLYING GAME (Fade in and out)
VO: We met up with Doris again, just as she was preparing to take flight… And take one step closer to her dream of becoming an astronaut.
DG: What I can say is that the view was spectacular. It was just breathtaking. I just praying, Lord be with me. Let me not get scared or anything, but just be with me. Like, it was amazing. Fantastic Spectacular. Like, yeah… I’m just out of words.
VO: Chimdiebere and his classmates from St Vincent had an entire plane just for their school.
CM: Are you scared to fly?
CH: No, I’m not scared at all!
CM: You’ll be as high as the clouds.
CH: Yes, I’m so sure. The clouds will be there. I’m going to be as high as the clouds. I’m going to be high flying on the plane. But I’m not scared at all, I’m sure of it.
CM: Most of the kids that come here, would they have had this opportunity at any other time in their lives?
VT: This opportunity is the opportunity for them. And most of our kids do definitely come from disadvantaged backgrounds. They will take in every little detail. So most of them have seem the airplane in the pictures, and has seen when we go out for outings, but has never been so close to go up in the air and fly.
CM: For those people who don’t get it, what would you say to them?
TW: The children in our area have very little opportunity because of where we stay. It’s incredibly poor. So for something like this to happen, for a child in our area… most of them, some of them haven’t even been in a car before. So it’s something that’s just enormous, and like I said to Felix, you’ve given my children, the children that we bring, the opportunity to dream, which is something they haven’t done in a very long time. And I think to have a dream is the first step to actioning something and making your dreams into a reality.
DG: It takes someone to do something for someone in order for that person to really see how important that thing is, like what impact that thing has on that person.
07:50 - 08:00 - MUSIC CUE: FLYING GAME

They approach the aircraft, because they’re fascinated by the big metal bird, and they want to be part of the experience. And that’s very much the founding area of this initiative. CM LINK: Organized by Felix Gosher and his friend musician Michael Ferguson, The Children’s Flight is an initiative to “Fly, Feed, Love, Inspire.” For many children, this is their first time ever on an airplane. VO: Michael Ferguson, co-founder of The Children’s Flight, explains further. CM: Why children and airplanes? MICHAEL FERGUSON (MF): Aviation is such a beacon of hope. Last year, we had some younger children. And some people say, “Man, these kids probably don’t get what’s happening. And they won’t remember the experience.” But I don’t believe that’s true. I think subconsciously, you take away something much bigger. I think it’s got such a lifelong impact on the children. VO: On 1 September, at Grand Central Airport in Midrand, Felix and Michael’s initiative took to the skies. CM LINK: Children come from all parts of Johannesburg to attend The Children’s Flight, representing different schools, organizations, and centers. Since the inaugural event last year, the event has almost tripled in size. 05:25 - 06:50 - MUSIC CUE: FLYING GAME (Fade in and out) VO: We met up with Doris again, just as she was preparing to take flight… And take one step closer to her dream of becoming an astronaut. DG: What I can say is that the view was spectacular. It was just breathtaking. I just praying, Lord be with me. Let me not get scared or anything, but just be with me. Like, it was amazing. Fantastic Spectacular. Like, yeah… I’m just out of words. VO: Chimdiebere and his classmates from St Vincent had an entire plane just for their school. CM: Are you scared to fly? CH: No, I’m not scared at all! CM: You’ll be as high as the clouds. CH: Yes, I’m so sure. The clouds will be there. I’m going to be as high as the clouds. I’m going to be high flying on the plane. But I’m not scared at all, I’m sure of it. CM: Most of the kids that come here, would they have had this opportunity at any other time in their lives? VT: This opportunity is the opportunity for them. And most of our kids do definitely come from disadvantaged backgrounds. They will take in every little detail. So most of them have seem the airplane in the pictures, and has seen when we go out for outings, but has never been so close to go up in the air and fly. CM: For those people who don’t get it, what would you say to them? TW: The children in our area have very little opportunity because of where we stay. It’s incredibly poor. So for something like this to happen, for a child in our area… most of them, some of them haven’t even been in a car before. So it’s something that’s just enormous, and like I said to Felix, you’ve given my children, the children that we bring, the opportunity to dream, which is something they haven’t done in a very long time. And I think to have a dream is the first step to actioning something and making your dreams into a reality. DG: It takes someone to do something for someone in order for that person to really see how important that thing is, like what impact that thing has on that person. 07:50 - 08:00 - MUSIC CUE: FLYING GAME

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): Volunteer pilots prepare for hundreds of children from all over Johannesburg -- to take to the sky for the first time and inspire a generation of children with the gift of flight.
metadata.Unique Selling Point: Working closely with the co-founders of the Children’s Flight, we’ll get access to various flights throughout the event, as well as coordinate having camera crew accompanying our young case studies as they take to the skies for the very first time.
metadata.Summary: Many people don’t think anything of hopping on a flight to Cape Town or Durban for the weekend. But for underprivileged children around Johannesburg, just getting to set foot on an airfield can be an awe-striking experience and a dream come true. The organizers behind The Children’s Flight aim to do just that with their annual event. Children from all parts of Johannesburg, all backgrounds, and all abilities are invited to the airport to experience their first flight. Felix Gosher and Michael Ferguson, the co-founders of the event, say it’s nearly tripled in size since last year (from 126 kids to nearly 400), and the response from the community has been truly remarkable. In this segment, we’ll spend a day in the life with two young people living in difficult circumstances -- 16 year old Doris in the mining township of Durban deep, whose mother has polio, and her family unable to pay her school fees; and 8 year old Chimdiebere, deaf since birth and living in Tembisa with a large family that often overlooks him, leaving him with rarely enough on the table to keep him from being hungry. Overcoming very difficult odds, they both excel in their studies, have dreams for professional careers (Doris as an astronaut and Chimdiebere as a policeman) and will be taking part in the Children’s Flight on 1 September. We’ll be with them the first time they set foot on an airplane and have an up close and personal look at how this experience inspires them in their personal lives to keep reaching for their dreams.
metadata.Further information: On the outskirts of Johannesburg in the township of Durban Deep lives sixteen year old Doris. Living in a garage by a row of old mining houses, Doris and her family do not have electricity or water. Her mother has polio, and recently, Doris was thrown out of school after her family was unable to pay the fees. However, after her story spread around the community, a good Samaritan stepped up to pay the fees and get Doris back in school. The local newspaper, the Roodeport Record, picked up on the story, and another school actually offered to sponsor Doris’s fees, uniform, and transport. Against many odds, Doris still attends school regularly and has dreams of becoming an astronaut. On Friday, 1 September, Doris will take one step closer to realizing her dream when she and hundreds of other children from in and around Johannesburg descend on Grand Central Airport in Midrand for the Children’s Flight. Organized by career pilot Felix Gosher and his close friend, musician Michael Ferguson, the Children’s Flight is a Mandela Day initiative to “Fly, Feed, Love, Inspire” underprivileged children from various backgrounds and let them experience aviation up close, as well as see the world from a different perspective. Michael and Felix each credit each other with the origin of the event, but the story goes that Michael was inspired to write a song, “Paper Planes,” after hearing about Felix’s travels across Africa. The song is the story of a child with a dream to fly. Felix says he would land his airplane in various remote parts of the continent and would always be struck by how children would run up to it, amazed by the fact that it seemed to defy gravity and take him off to exotic places. According to Michael, “We didn’t plan on writing that song… he told me his story about becoming a pilot, and after that, we just sort of wrote [it].” Both Felix and Michael were satisfied with the final product, but initially, nothing more came of it. It was only on a work trip flying through central Africa that Felix realized, what good is inspiration if you don’t share it with others? From there, he and Michael decided that the thing they could give others was the gift of flight, and thus the Children’s Flight was born. Now in its second year, the event has nearly tripled in size (400 kids will attend in 2017), and the energy amongst the youngsters is palpable. They come from all parts of the city. Chimdiebere is 8 years old, and this will be his first time flying. His favorite subject in school is math, and he wants to be a policeman when he grows up. He lives with his large family in Tembisa, up to eight members sharing the same small house, and makes the long commute in to school every day in Illovo. However, Chimdiebere’s experience will be different than most other kids, because he’s deaf. Though he has 2 cochlear implants, he can only hear very loud noises (dogs barking, doors slamming, and airplanes). At St Vincent’s School for the Deaf, where he attends, the teachers have to make sure he’s eaten and can function properly for the day, because food is scarce at home. Often, the only meals he will get for the day will be at the school. His family doesn’t use sign language, so when he goes home, there’s no one to talk to, and he typically only plays with his baby brother. In spite of all this, he’s doing very well in school and is quite popular. An event like Children’s Flight brings together kids like Doris and Chimdiebere, and the pilots and other volunteers who give their time hope that it will inspire them to dream and understand that dreams can be within striking distance if you work at it. Pilots like Werner Nel demonstrate that. He began training to become a pilot in 2007. His career began as a private pilot with the ultimate goal of becoming a commercial pilot. However, in October 2009, he was involved in a motorcycle accident that nearly took his life. Though he survived, doctors had to amputate his right leg. He was devastated at the prospect that his flying career may be over. But he didn’t let that stop him. After three years of physical therapy and numerous operations, he gained his commercial pilot’s license in 2012 and secured a job as a pilot instructor. He is still able to fly and now also works as an aerobatic pilot. His advice to anyone who asks about his experience -- and especially the kids who will be at Children’s Flight -- is: “Never give up and always remember, if you give your 100%, you will have endless possibilities.” Doris (awaiting surname from contact).
